title: What is known about 1RB1LE_1LC0RA_0RF0LD_1LE1LA_1RC0LB_---1RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LE_1LC0RA_0RF0LD_1LE1LA_1RC0LB_---1RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and Collatz-like. Write a = 10, b = 110. At the moments the head, in B, extends the tape to the left, the tape is B> 0 0 a^k b a^m 1 (two blocks, one marker) or B> 0 0 a^k b a^m b a^n 1 (three blocks). The first block doubles, k → 2k + 3, and takes k + 2 pairs from the second block each time; when the second block is too short the marker runs off the end and the blocks are rebuilt from what is left. All of this is one explicit map on the lists [k, m] and [k, m, n] (eight cases, below). The map is fitted: it agrees with a direct run of the machine on 1,053 small lists and with the run from blank tape at all 214 marker moments of the first 3.7·107 steps, but it is not proved. Proved in Lean: blank tape reaches the list [1, 1, 1] at step 72, and a block with no marker halts whatever its length. By the map, a block with no marker is produced exactly from two equal blocks [k, k], so the machine halts if and only if the orbit of [1, 1, 1] ever meets [k, k]. It has not in 3·108 iterations, where the blocks are numbers of about 1,000 bits; no residue pattern excludes it. The community tracker lists this machine as a cryptid (halting reduces to a Collatz-like question), which is what this map shows.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 15,585 cells have been visited and 7,792 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.229). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.478).

claims.title: The sweeps
claims.text: D runs left over pairs carrying the marker cell (L (01)^n D> 1 R → L D> 1 (01)^n R, 4 steps a pair), and A and B run right over pairs. Generated by py/rules.py.

claims.title: Blank tape reaches the marker list [1, 1, 1]
claims.text: After 72 steps from blank tape the configuration is B> 0 0 a b a b a 1 with blank tape on both sides: the list [1, 1, 1]. Evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: A block with no marker halts
claims.text: For every N, the configuration B> 0 0 a^N 1 (blank on both sides) halts, after 2N + 7 steps: F and C walk right over the pairs and F reads the blank cell after the tape. Proved for all N; nothing is assumed.

claims.title: The map on marker lists
claims.text:
From one marker moment to the next (fitted):
  • [k, m] with m ≥ k+2 → [2k+3, m−k−2] (the marker doubles);
  • [k, k+1] → [1, 2k+3, 1];
  • [k, k] → [2k+3], a block with no marker, which halts;
  • [k, m] with m < k: [k−m, 2m+3] if k−m is odd, [1, k−m−1, 2m+3] if it is even;
  • [k, m, n] with n odd: [2k+3, m−k−2, n] if m ≥ k+2; [1, 2k+n+4] if m ≤ k; [1, 4k+n+10] if m = k+1.
From [1, 1, 1] only these lists occur (the third block is always odd, the first always odd). This is a fit to simulations, not a theorem.

claims.title: The map agrees with the machine
claims.text: py/map.py table: a direct run of the machine from each list [k, m] and [k, m, n] with k < 9, m < 13, n < 8 gives the list the formulas predict (1,053 lists; for n even the formulas differ and are in the script). py/map.py check 4e7: from blank tape the machine passes through exactly the orbit of [1, 1, 1] at all 214 marker moments up to step 36,965,083, where the list is [1021, 819].

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>8</sup> iterations of the map
claims.text: Iterating the fitted map with exact integers from [1, 1, 1]: no list [k, k] in 3·108 iterations (py/map.py far 3e8, a few minutes); the blocks are then numbers of about 1,000 bits. This says the machine does not halt for an astronomically long time if the fitted map is right.

claims.title: No residue pattern excludes a halt
claims.text: In the orbit k is always odd and m changes parity at each doubling, so m = k is not excluded by parity; and k − m ≡ 0 occurs at the expected rate modulo each of 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48 (3·10<sup>6</sup> iterations). The chance of an exact hit shrinks as the blocks grow, so a halt looks very unlikely, but that is the usual heuristic for Collatz-like maps, not a proof.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. If the fitted map is right, it is the question whether the orbit of [1, 1, 1] ever meets a list of two equal blocks [k, k]; a Collatz-like question. The map itself still has to be proved (the doubling pass by induction, and the overflow cases).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 15,585 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A block of pairs and a marker
html: Write a for the pair 10 and b for 110. Stop the simulator whenever the head, in B, steps onto a new cell at the left end. The tape is then a block of pairs cut by one or two markers:
B> 0 0 a^k b a^m 1   or   B> 0 0 a^k b a^m b a^n 1

So the state of the machine at these moments is a short list of numbers, [k, m] or [k, m, n]. From blank tape the first one is [1, 1, 1], at step 72 (proved). Then: [1, 7], [5, 4], [1, 11], [5, 8], [13, 1], [1, 11, 5], [5, 8, 5], [13, 1, 5], [1, 35], [5, 32], [13, 25], [29, 10], [19, 23], [41, 2], ...

sections.heading: Doubling, and running off the end
html: Doubling. If the second block has room (m ≥ k + 2), the marker moves to twice its distance: [k, m] → [2k + 3, m − k − 2]. A third block, if there is one, just waits. From k = 1 the first block is 1, 5, 13, 29, 61, 125, ...

Running off. If the second block is too short (m < k), the doubling stops part way. With one marker, the k − m pairs that were not doubled become the new first block when that number is odd, [k − m, 2m + 3]; when it is even a fresh marker starts at the left and there are two markers, [1, k − m − 1, 2m + 3]. With two markers everything is wiped into one block with a fresh marker, [1, 2k + n + 4]. Two edge cases: [k, k + 1] → [1, 2k + 3, 1], and [k, k + 1, n] → [1, 4k + n + 10].
Example: [29, 10] has m < k and 29 − 10 = 19 is odd, so the next list is [19, 23]. Then [41, 2] → [39, 7] → (39 − 7 = 32 is even) [1, 31, 17].
These formulas are a fit. They were checked against the machine itself on 1,053 small lists and along the real run (214 marker moments, 3.7·107 steps), but they are not proved.

sections.heading: Two equal blocks
html: A block with no marker at all, B> 0 0 a^N 1, halts: the head walks right over the pairs, steps past the end of the tape and the machine stops. This is proved in Lean for every N (single_halts).

In the map, a block with no marker comes from exactly one kind of list: two equal blocks, [k, k] → [2k + 3]. (The doubling pass then uses up the second block exactly and swallows the marker.) So the machine halts if and only if the run ever reaches two equal blocks — assuming the fitted map.

The first block is always odd; the second changes parity at every doubling; no small modulus separates them. After 3·108 iterations the blocks are numbers of about 1,000 bits and no hit has occurred. Whether one ever does is a Collatz-like question: nobody knows how to decide such things, which is why the community calls this machine a cryptid.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.229). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.478).
After 109 steps the tape spans 15,585 cells (998 left of the start, 10,012 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A block of pairs 10 cut by markers 110. Each pass doubles the first block (k -> 2k+3) at the cost of the second; when the second is too short the marker runs off and the blocks are rebuilt. The whole run is the orbit of an explicit map on lists of two or three block sizes (fitted, checked against the machine, not proved), and it halts iff the orbit meets two equal blocks [k, k]: no hit in 3*10^8 iterations. Open, Collatz-like (a cryptid).
family: doubling marker in a growing block (Collatz-like map on block sizes)
